title: How Fentanyl Ended a Hostage Crisis — and Killed 120 People
fullText: April 21st, 2016. At 6:07 in the morning, a member of the household staff at Paisley Park, the private Minnesota estate of one of the bestselling musicians in American history, presses the call button for the estate's private elevator. Nothing happens. He presses it again. Still nothing. The elevator sits motionless, the doors sealed. No hum of machinery, no answer of any kind. And with each passing second, the silence starts to feel less like a malfunction and more like a warning. After several long minutes, unable to wait any longer, the staff member forces the doors open by hand. Inside, crumpled on the floor, is Prince. He has been dead for hours. Investigators searching the property in the days that follow find pills scattered through the [music] house, hidden inside vitamin bottles and aspirin containers stamped with a familiar prescription code, the kind millions of Americans would recognize on site and trust without a second thought. Friends and staff later describe a man who had quietly been struggling with hip and knee pain from decades of high energy performances. A private struggle almost nobody around him fully understood. The toxicology report when it finally comes back does not match a single one of those labels on the pills found in his home. Prince did not die from what those pills claimed to be. He died from something else entirely. Something quietly slipped inside them. Something so potent that the amount required to end his life would have been barely visible resting in the palm of a hand. The news breaks within hours and does not stay contained to entertainment coverage for long. Radio stations interrupt their programming. Tribute crowds gather outside Paisley Park within the day. Public health officials scramble to explain to a stunned public how one of the most recognizable musicians alive could be killed by a substance almost nobody outside a hospital or a DEA briefing room had ever heard of. Reporters asked the same question again and again in the days that follow. What exactly is fentinil? And how did it end up in a pill that looked so convincingly like something else? Within a few years, that same substance would become the leading cause of death for young Americans nationwide, ahead of car accidents, ahead of gun violence, ahead of every other single cause on the list. This is not a story about a cartel invention or a jungle plant smuggled across an ocean. It is the story of a molecule built by one of the most prolific pharmaceutical chemists of the 20th century in a small Belgian laboratory to make surgery safer decades before it ever touched a counterfeit [music] pill. So, how does a drug trusted by hospitals for more than half a century become the substance behind one of the most famous accidental deaths in music history? The story begins in 1959 [music] in Belgium, Paul Jansen was still in his 20s when he first started making a name for himself in pharmaceutical research. Born in 1926 in the Belgian town of Turnout, the son of a small town physician who had built his own modest pharmaceutical business, Yansen borrowed the equivalent of 50,000 Belgian Franks from his father in 1953 and opened a research laboratory of his own. The operation was almost comically humble at first. A small lab set up inside his family's own company building. Within 2 years, that scrappy lab had produced its first drug, a treatment for menstrual pain. It would not be the last. Colleagues who worked alongside Yansen described a man who seemed to daydream in molecules, doodling new chemical structures during meetings out of pure restlessness. Over his career, his laboratory would eventually be credited with developing dozens of major pharmaceuticals. And by some counts, no single individual in the history of the industry would ever match his output. In 1959, Johnson and his team set out to improve on an existing opioid painkiller called [music] Pthodine, sold under the brand name Demoril. Hunting for something faster acting and far more potent than morphine, they tested candidate compounds on lab mice using a simple, brutal method, placing the animals on a heated plate and slowly raising the temperature to see how long it took before pain finally registered. One of the molecules that came out of that testing barely registered as painful to the mice at all, even at far higher plate [music] temperatures than morphine could tolerate. Johnson's team had found something extraordinary. They just did not yet have a name for it. The molecule receives a formal chemical name eventually, fennel piperine derivative, later shortened in common use to fentinyl. When Johnson pharmaceutica brings it to market as an injectable surgical anesthetic in the early 1960s, they call it sublimase. It is a fitting product for the era. A drug roughly 100 times more potent than morphine by weight. So potent that as little as 2 mg, [music] an amount that can sit on the tip of a pencil is enough to be fatal to an average adult with no tolerance. Within a few years, the company that discovered it becomes something much bigger than a small Belgian lab. In 1961, the American conglomerate Johnson and Johnson acquires Johnson Pharmaceutica outright and fentinyl becomes one of its most quietly profitable assets. Doctors have every reason to love the new drug. Older opioids like morphine can cause blood pressure to crash dramatically during surgery, [music] a dangerous complication in patients whose hearts are already under strain. Fentinyl does not do this nearly as severely, making it far safer for high-risk cardiac surgery patients specifically, and its extremely fast onset meant anesthesiologists could control a patient's depth of sedation with a precision older opioid simply could not match, dialing the dose up or down almost in real time as a procedure unfolded. Anesthesiologists across Europe and then the United States adopt a technique combining fentinyl with a seditive [music] called dropperidal. A combination known as neuralttp anesthesia that becomes standard practice in operating rooms on both sides of the Atlantic through the 1960s and '7s. Trade journals of the era describe it in almost celebratory terms. a genuine leap forward for a specialty that had gone decades relying on the same handful of imperfect tools. By the time the drug earns full approval for general anesthesia use in the United States, it has already become, in the words of physicians who worked with it, one of the most versatile tools in the entire pharmacy. reached for in everything from routine outpatient procedures [music] to the most delicate open heart surgeries in the country. And then in August of 1990, Fentinel leaves the operating room behind almost entirely. The Food and Drug Administration approves Durigesic, a fentinel skin patch designed to release a slow, continuous dose over a full 72 hours. developed specifically for cancer patients suffering chronic unrelenting pain that pills alone could not manage. For the first time, a patient dying of cancer could wear a patch on their arm and go days without thinking about the clock, without waking at 3:00 in the morning for another dose. It is by nearly every clinical measure a genuine mercy. But there was a problem. A drug this potent, delivered continuously through the skin, is also a drug that is extraordinarily easy to misuse and extraordinarily unforgiving when misused. Healthare workers, the very people trusted to administer fentinel safely, would go on to record some of the highest rates of occupational opioid addiction of any profession. [music] anesthesiologists and operating room nurses among them simply because of how much access they had to it siphoning small amounts from vials meant for patients without anyone noticing for months or years at a time. Patients and diverters learned they could chew a used durigic patch or freeze one and extract its remaining gel to release days worth of drug all at once, turning a slowrelease medical device into an improvised, dangerously concentrated dose. And as early as 1979, a chemist working outside any legitimate laboratory synthesized a fentinel analog specifically designed [music] to be more potent than fentinyl itself. sold on the street under the name China White, precisely engineered to slip past the legal definition of the scheduled drug it was copying. The Drug Enforcement Administration scrambled to schedule that specific molecule. Clandestine chemists simply tweaked the structure [music] again and made a new one, a pattern of legal cat and mouse that would repeat itself in one form or another for the next four decades. Here is the part most people never learn, and it is the hinge on which the entire modern crisis turns. Pharmaceutical fentinyl's danger had always been contained by hospitals, prescriptions, and locked cabinets. But fentinyl, the molecule, does not need a poppy field. [music] Heroin needs opium poppies, acorage, a growing season, a harvest that can be located from the air and burned. Cocaine [music] needs cocoa leaf, mountain sides, tropical climate. Fentinyl needs none of that. It can be synthesized entirely from industrial chemical precursors in a lab the size of a garage by a chemist with the right training and a shopping [music] list rather than a farm. For the first time in the history of the modern drug trade, an opioid many times more potent than heroin could be manufactured with no agricultural bottleneck at all and no crop for satellites or drug agents to [music] find and destroy. By the 2010s, that fact had reshaped the entire supply chain. Following a 1979 street debut and a slow underground spread through the following decades, [music] illicit fentinel synthesis exploded once precursor chemical suppliers, many operating openly out of China, began shipping the building blocks to organized manufacturing networks, often disguised on shipping manifests as ordinary industrial [music] chemicals bound for unrelated commercial use. sometimes labeled as flavoring agents or plastics additives to slip past customs inspection. After China moved in 2019 to formally schedule fentinel and its analoges as a class, much of that chemical trade shifted toward Mexican cartels, chiefly the Sinaloa cartel and cartel Jalisco Noea Generation, who imported the precursor chemicals and ran the cooking operations themselves, effectively vertically integrating a drug trade that had once required farmers, harvesters, refiners, and smugglers all working in sequence. each link a potential point of failure the cartels no longer had to worry about. Clandestine chemists working in makeshift labs mix, press, and dye the finished powder into pills stamped to look identical to legitimate pharmaceutical oxycodone, a counterfeit known on the street simply as Blues or M30 pills for the number stamped on their face. Because fentinil is active at doses measured in micrograms rather than milligs, mixing a batch evenly is nearly impossible even for a careful chemist. Which means two pills pressed minutes apart on the very same machine can carry wildly different amounts of the drug, one harmless, [music] the next one lethal. The workers running these operations are themselves routinely poisoned by the very product they are manufacturing, absorbing dangerous exposure through careless handling in makeshift labs with none of the safety infrastructure, the ventilation, the protective equipment of a real pharmaceutical plant. The scale this reaches is almost impossible to picture in ordinary terms. So picture it this way instead. A single kilogram of pure fentinyl, roughly the weight of a bag of sugar, contains something on the order of 500,000 [music] potentially lethal doses. A quantity that would once have required an entire cocoa or poppy harvest to approach and can now be cooked in a single batch. In one DEA raid in Queens, New York, agents found an industrial pill press running out of an ordinary residential living room, stamping out counterfeit tablets in a house sitting directly across the street from a public elementary school. In 2023 alone, law enforcement agencies nationwide, federal, state, and local combined, seized more than 115 million counterfeit fentinyl pills, along with thousands of pounds of fentinyl powder in operations across the country. [music] The DEA's own share of that total alone, topping 77 million pills. Officials in Texas alone reported seizing enough fentinyl in a single year to theoretically kill 200 million people. A number roughly 2/3 of the entire population of the United States from the seizures of a single state in a single year. These are not hypothetical numbers built for shock value. They are seizure totals. Meaning they represent only the fraction of the supply that got caught. the fraction law enforcement actually saw before it reached a street corner, a party, or a counterfeit prescription bottle. [music] And the human cost behind those numbers is staggering on its own terms. And it did not arrive gradually. In 2013, synthetic opioids, overwhelmingly illicit fentinyl, were linked [music] to roughly 3,100 American deaths in a single year, a number that barely registered as a national crisis at the time. By 2023, that number had risen to 72,776, more than a 23-fold increase in exactly one decade. And synthetic opioids alone accounted for close to 70% of all overdose deaths recorded that year. Fentinyl overdose is now the leading cause of death for Americans between the ages of 18 and 44, ahead of car accidents, ahead of gun violence, ahead of every other single cause on the list. A grim distinction that would have been unthinkable to most public health officials as recently as 2010, and one that Prince's death had quietly foreshadowed years before the statistics ever caught up with it. Among Americans aged 25 to 34 specifically, fentinyl linked deaths alone accounted for more than 16,000 [music] fatalities in 2023. A generation disproportionately caught in the crossfire of a drug supply few of them ever intended to [music] encounter. In recent years, fentinyl has increasingly turned up mixed into an animal tranquilizer called xylazine, a combination street users call tran, [music] which does not respond to standard overdose reversal medication and causes severe disfiguring [music] skin wounds in long-term users, adding an entirely new medical crisis on top of the overdose numbers themselves. Fentinel did not simply replace heroin as the country's dominant opioid. Fentinel restructured the entire architecture of the American drug crisis because it was the first major opioid in history that never needed a farm. Even as the panic around the drug reached its peak, some of the country's leading toxicologists pushed back hard against the specific claims spreading through police departments and news coverage, insisting that fear itself was becoming a public health problem of its own. Their warnings were largely drowned out for years by louder, more viral stories. If you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. We cover stories like this every week, and you will not want to miss what comes next. In the spring of 2016, two narcotics detectives in Atlantic County, New Jersey, field test a bag of suspected heroin recovered during an investigation. following the same basic procedure they had followed hundreds of times before, puncturing the bag and exposing it briefly to open air. Within minutes, both are on the ground. Both are rushed to the hospital and both recover. Their account of the experience filmed for what they were told was internal training material is instead released by the DEA in June of 2016 as a nationwide roll call video shared and reshared by police unions, local news affiliates, and worried departments hundreds of miles away who had never encountered anything like it. The video accompanies a nationwide warning to every law enforcement agency in the country stating plainly that a very small amount of fentinyl ingested or absorbed through the skin [music] can kill. Departments across the country respond exactly as you would expect people to respond to a credible warning from their own federal drug agency. They buy specialized protective gear. Some of it later described by toxicologists as an outright scam preying on genuine fear. They adopt hazmat level protocols for approaching suspected fentinil requiring full body suits and respirators for what used to be routine evidence collection and officers are trained to treat the mere sight of unknown powder as a potentially lethal threat to their own lives. That fear does not stay contained to training rooms. Researchers studying real world overdose response have found that professional responders genuinely afraid for their own safety sometimes hesitate before administering the lock zone or even approaching an unconscious overdose victim delaying the exact intervention [music] that saves lives. A drug engineered in 1959 specifically to make patients safer during surgery had by pure accident of media coverage helped make some of the responders meant to save overdose victims more hesitant to reach them in time. And here is a twist. Almost nobody connects to the current crisis. Fentinil has a molecular relative developed by researchers working in the same scientific lineage. one that is roughly 10,000 times more potent than morphine and 100 times more potent than fentinil itself. Carfentinil was developed as a large animal tranquilizer. Potent enough to sedate an elephant with a fraction of a milligram and it has never been approved for any use in humans at all. Its only legitimate application confined to veterinary medicine for the very largest animals on the planet. In October of 2002, Chetchin [music] separatists, armed with explosives and automatic weapons, seized a crowded Moscow theater [music] during a soldout performance, taking more than 800 hostages and wiring the auditorium with bombs. For nearly 3 days, the siege held the world's attention. Negotiations stalling, deadlines passing, families gathered outside a security perimeter with no information at all. Before dawn on the fourth day, Russian special forces made their move, not with a direct assault, but by pumping an unidentified aerosol through the building's ventilation system. Inside the darkened theater, hostages and hostage takers alike began losing consciousness within minutes, collapsing in their seats with no warning and no time to react. Special forces then stormed the building and killed every remaining gunman. Russian authorities never fully disclosed what the gas [music] contained beyond confirming it involved fentinyl related compounds and for a decade the world was left to guess. In 2012, British scientists analyzing clothing and blood samples from surviving hostages finally confirmed the aerosol was a mixture of carfentinyl and a related surgical anesthetic rementyl. [music] The operation killed every one of the hostage takers and it also killed somewhere between 125 and 170 of the hostages themselves. Largely because medical crews on the ground positioned outside without any warning of what they were about to face were never told what compound they needed to reverse and could not administer the right antidote in time to the people carried out unconscious around them. A molecule descended from the same 1950s research that made surgery safer had within a single generation become a chemical weapon used by a national government against [music] its own citizens. Officially banned under the Chemical Weapons Convention and used anyway. Through the 2000s [music] and into the 2010s, illicit fentinel accumulates a long list of street names. Apache, dance fever, tango, [music] and cash, China White. Each one obscuring the actual drug hidden inside it. A naming pattern deliberately designed to keep buyers from realizing exactly what they were purchasing. In the fall of 2022, a new wave of alarms sweeps through American media around so-called rainbow fentinel, brightly colored pills and powder that the Drug Enforcement Administration publicly warned could be a deliberate effort to target children ahead of Halloween. Photos of candy colored pills in shades of pink, blue, and green circulated through school district newsletters and local news broadcasts within days. Parents warned to check their children's Halloween candy for hidden narcotics. Some schools sending automated alerts home to every family on the roster. It followed unmistakably the same shape as the contact overdose panic years earlier. A dramatic federal warning, rapid viral spread, and very little verified evidence behind the most alarming version of the story. Toxicologists who studied the actual coloring later noted it more plausibly reflected branding [music] and manufacturing choices among rival trafficking networks competing for market share. The same reason serial boxes come in different colors rather than any coordinated plan to hook children specifically. And by this point in the crisis, fentinil is no longer confined to what anyone would [music] call the opioid market at all. Public health labs increasingly find it mixed into cocaine, methamphetamine, and counterfeit prescription pills sold as Xanax or Adderall. Meaning people who believe they are using an entirely different drug, sometimes for the first time in their lives, are gambling with a substance where 2 millig is the difference between a normal night and a funeral. Here is the playbook, and longtime followers of channels like this one will recognize the shape of it immediately because it is nearly identical to the myth that [music] grew up decades earlier around another feared street drug, PCP, and its supposed superhuman strength. In both cases, a handful of dramatic unverified incidents get amplified by well-intentioned officials into sweeping public warnings. In both cases, those warnings calcify into institutional training and public belief long before anyone actually tests the underlying science. And in both cases, when scientists finally do test it, the myth collapses almost completely. In 2017, the American College of Medical Toxicology and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology issue a joint position statement addressing the [music] wave of police contact overdose claims directly. They had been watching the videos accumulate for months, one department after another, reporting officers going down after nothing more than brushing powder off a sleeve. and [music] enough of their own members were being asked to weigh in, sometimes by reporters, sometimes by worried police chiefs looking for cover, that the organizations decided the question could no longer be answered case by case. Their conclusion is blunt. The risk of clinically significant exposure to emergency responders from passive skin contact or brief airborne exposure is, [music] in their words, essentially zero. And no medically substantiated case of a first responder overdosing from incidental contact has ever been documented. Not one out of the dozens of viral videos and news [music] segments that had by then aired across the country. Their math is almost comically decisive. Even in the most extreme scenario, researchers could construct both palms of a person's hands completely covered in pharmaceutical-grade fentinyl patches specifically engineered to maximize skin absorption. It would still take roughly 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms of the drug. [music] A therapeutic dose, not a lethal one. Loose powder brushed off a sleeve or a uniform would absorb dramatically slower than that best case engineered scenario. Toxicologists including Dr. Ryan Marino, Dr. Andrew Stalbark, and Dr. David Jerling have repeatedly examined viral police contact overdose videos and reached the same conclusion every time. The specific symptoms described, sudden dizziness, a racing heart, difficulty breathing, a rapid loss of consciousness within seconds of contact do not match how opioid toxicity actually presents in the human body. Real opioid overdose is a slow, progressive slide into unresponsive, shallow breathing over minutes, not an instantaneous collapse. What these officers were describing instead matches something else entirely. A panic response triggered by a very real, very justified fear of a genuinely deadly drug. Dr. Stalach's advice for anyone who does get fentinyl powder on their skin is almost anticlimactic by comparison to the fear it generates. Wash it off with water and otherwise do not worry about it at all. None of this makes fentinyl less dangerous in the way that actually kills [music] tens of thousands of Americans every year through injection, [music] through snorting, through smoking, through swallowing a counterfeit pill. someone believed was something else. What it means is that an entirely separate avoidable danger built on a story that was never true had been layered on top of a real one. And the myth version was the one that spread [music] the furthest and fastest. And the pattern has not stopped repeating. The same institutional reflex that spread the contact overdose myth after 2016 [music] produced the rainbow fentinel candy panic in 2022. And researchers who study drugrelated media coverage expect it to produce another version of the same story the next time an unfamiliar substance frightens the public. The myth did not die when the original claims were debunked. It is simply waiting for its next drug. Globally, the crisis this molecule created remains overwhelmingly concentrated in North America, in the United States and Canada specifically, [music] in a way that sets fentinel apart from nearly every other drug this channel has covered. European nations working with a differently structured heroin supply and different border geography have so far avoided anything close to the scale of contamination and death seen north of the Mexican border. Though health officials there watch the American numbers closely, aware that the same chemistry and the same lack of an agricultural bottleneck could travel anywhere precursor chemicals can be shipped and that a supply chain built once can be redirected almost overnight to a new market. Public health responses have shifted hard in recent years [music] toward reducing the myth's real world harm alongside the drug's own. In 2023, the Food and Drug Administration approved over-the-counter sales of Nlloxxone under the brand name [music] Naran, removing the prescription barrier that had slowed emergency access for years. A decision public health officials had pushed for over the preceding decade as overdose deaths climbed year after year with no sign of leveling off. A growing number of states have decriminalized fentinel test strips, cheap paper tools that let users check whether a supply is contaminated before it is too late. Though several states still classify the strips as illegal drug paraphernalia, a legal holdover from an earlier era of drug policy that critics argue costs lives it could otherwise save. School nurses in some districts now keep Nlloxxone in the same cabinet as the Epipens, a small but telling sign of how far the crisis has reached into ordinary institutions. And that same year, the United States and China announced [music] a renewed agreement specifically targeting the precursor chemical trade that feeds cartel production. an attempt to choke off the supply chain at its earliest, least visible link long before it ever reaches a clandestine lab in Mexico or a pill press in a residential living room. It was there in a small Belgian laboratory in 1959 in a molecule tested on the reaction time of mice on a heating plate. It was there in an operating room in the 1960s, keeping a cardiac patients blood pressure steady when older drugs could not. It was there on a cancer patient's arm in 1990 in a patch that finally let someone sleep through the night without pain. It was there in a Moscow theater in 2002, turned from a mercy into a weapon, killing the very people it was meant to save. It was there in Prince's home in 2016, hidden inside a pill that never touched a real pharmacy. It was there on a New Jersey roadside in a story that spread across the country and was never actually true. At least not in the way it was told. It is there in a brightly colored pill mistaken for children's candy in 2022. in a warning that outran the evidence [music] exactly the way the last one did. It is there today. Cut into a fake blue pill stamped to look exactly like a prescription oxycodone. Sold to someone who has never heard the name Paul [music] Jansen and will never get the chance to. A molecule built to make pain disappear became within a single human lifetime the deadliest drug crisis this country has [music] ever recorded. and one of the most persistent unfounded fears among the very people trying to stop it. If this story surprised you, do me a favor and hit subscribe and tell me in the comments what city you are watching from and whether Fentinil has made the news where you live.
